quickId: Glossy evergreen leaves, finely toothed, smaller and narrower than japonica camellia
Blooms in fall (Oct–Dec), unlike japonicas that bloom mid-winter to spring
Ruffled white double flowers with yellow center; round green buds
lookalikes: Japonica camellia: larger, broader leaves; blooms later in winter and spring.
facts: Sasanquas are the fall-blooming camellias.
'Mine-no-yuki' is a common white double sasanqua in Lowcountry yards.
care: Prune right after blooming in late winter; later pruning removes next fall's buds. Check leaf undersides for tea scale (white fuzzy coating).

quickId: Multi-trunk vase shape with smooth, peeling, cinnamon-colored bark
Small oval leaves that turn orange and red in fall
Summer clusters of crinkled flowers; round seed capsules into winter
lookalikes: Its smooth, muscular multi-trunks are very distinctive. Few lookalikes in the yard.
facts: Blooms on new growth, so late-winter pruning doesn't cost flowers.
Topping all trunks at one height ("crepe murder") causes knuckles and weak sprouts.
care: Prune mid-Feb to early March. Remove suckers, dead and crossing branches, thin the interior, limb up the trunks. Take no more than about 1/4 of the canopy per year.

quickId: Low, clumping fan palm with no tall trunk; trunks creep along the ground
Silvery blue-green fan-shaped leaves
Leaf stems lined with small sharp teeth (the "saw")
lookalikes: Blue Mediterranean fan palm: stiffer, more deeply split leaves and short upright trunks. Dwarf palmetto (Sabal minor): smooth stems, greener.
facts: Native to the Southeast coast and tolerant of drought, heat, salt, and sandy soil.
The silver form is prized in Lowcountry landscaping.
care: Once a year, cut dead brown fronds at the base. Wear gloves. Never remove green fronds.

quickId: Rosette of stiff, narrow, dark-green sword-like leaves on a short trunk
Needle-sharp leaf tips
Fine saw-toothed leaf edges that feel rough
lookalikes: Spanish dagger / mound lily (Yucca gloriosa): wider, bluer, flexible leaves with smooth edges and softer tips. Often blooms in fall.
facts: Native along the Southeast coast.
Tall spikes of creamy white flowers in late spring or early summer.
Trunks can reach 8–10 ft. Cut pieces root easily.
care: Mind the tips near walkways; clipping the points is fine. Remove dead lower leaves with loppers, long sleeves, and eye protection.

quickId: Glossy, leathery oval leaves in opposite pairs
Leaves often a bit wavy or cupped, with a pale midrib
Blue-black berries in fall and winter
lookalikes: Yaupon holly has much smaller leaves; sweet olive often has toothed leaves.
facts: One of the most common foundation and hedge shrubs in coastal SC.
Considered invasive in SC: birds spread its berries.
Strong-scented white flower clusters in late spring.
care: Light shaping anytime in the growing season, narrower at top than bottom. Hard rejuvenation in late winter. It tolerates a cut to 12–18 in. Pull seedlings.

quickId: Grows on salt marsh edges
Gray-green leaves; upper leaves narrow
Females turn silvery-white with fluffy seed tufts in fall
lookalikes: False willow (Baccharis angustifolia): narrower, willow-like leaves, same marshes and same fall show.
facts: Male and female plants are separate. Only females get fluffy.
Late flowers feed migrating monarchs.
Very salt-tolerant and helps stabilize marsh edges. Mildly toxic to livestock.
care: A wild native. Leave it be.

quickId: Tall, dense stands of broad, flat grass blades
Leaf edges are saw-toothed and will cut skin
Freshwater tidal marsh, often in old rice fields
lookalikes: Wild rice (Zizania aquatica): soft leaf edges and big airy seed heads in late summer. Cultivated rice doesn't persist in the wild here.
facts: Spreads by thick rhizomes into nearly pure stands.
A main plant that took over Waccamaw rice fields after cultivation ended.
Gives cover to marsh birds and wildlife.
care: Wear long sleeves walking through it.

quickId: Flared, buttressed trunk base, often standing in water
Cypress "knees" poking up around it
Soft needles that turn rusty-brown and drop in fall (a deciduous conifer)
lookalikes: Pond cypress (Taxodium ascendens): needles pressed close to twigs, more often in still ponds.
facts: Some Black River cypress are over 2,000 years old.
Big stumps on the Waccamaw are mostly from logging in the late 1800s and early 1900s.
The Spanish moss hanging on it is a bromeliad, not a moss, and doesn't harm the tree.
care: A wild native. Enjoy it from the water.

quickId: Small, smooth, oval leaves in opposite pairs along the stem
Leaf tips rounded, often with a tiny notch; edges never toothed
Dense, fine-textured shrub that shears into tidy hedges; brighter green than English boxwood
lookalikes: Japanese holly (Ilex crenata): leaves alternate (not paired) with tiny teeth on the edges. English boxwood: darker, more pointed leaves, struggles in coastal SC heat.
facts: Japanese boxwood handles Southern heat and humidity far better than English boxwood.
Leaves can turn bronze or yellowish in winter sun and green up in spring.
Crushed leaves have a faint musky smell some people dislike.
care: Shear lightly in late spring after the first flush of growth, and again in summer if needed. Avoid heavy trimming after September so new growth can harden before cold. Thin a few interior branches now and then so light and air reach the center. Keep mulch off the stems; boxwood hates wet feet.

quickId: Small, rounded, slightly fuzzy leaves alternating along arching, reddish-brown stems
New leaves purple or burgundy; older leaves often fade to green, especially in shade
Pink flowers with narrow, strap-like, ribbony petals, like a frayed tassel
lookalikes: Green-leaf loropetalum (white flowers) is the same species. Before it blooms, it can resemble cotoneaster or a small-leaf holly, but loropetalum's leaves are softer and slightly fuzzy, with no teeth.
facts: Main bloom is a heavy flush in early spring, with scattered flowers in fall like the one here.
Leaves on a purple-leaf plant often turn mostly green in shade, in summer heat, or on older growth.
Many varieties grow 10–15 ft if never pruned, far bigger than most people expect.
care: Prune right after the spring bloom. Shape by cutting individual branches back to a side branch rather than shearing into a ball. It also takes hard rejuvenation pruning well. It likes acidic, well-drained soil; yellowing leaves with green veins usually mean the soil is too alkaline.

quickId: Glossy, wavy leaves with sharp spines along the edges: the classic Christmas holly shape
Dark green center with a wide creamy-white border
Purplish tint on young stems and new growth; some leaves come out almost all cream
lookalikes: 'O. Spring' holly: a popular Southern variegated holly with yellow-gold borders and a more upright form. Native American holly (Ilex opaca): plain green, duller leaves with fewer spines.
facts: Holly plants are male or female; only females make red berries, and they need a male holly nearby.
Variegated leaves have less green to make food, so the plant grows slower than plain green holly.
English holly prefers cooler summers. In coastal SC it does best with afternoon shade and good drainage.
care: Cut off any branch that reverts to all-green leaves, since it will outgrow the variegated part. Prune lightly in late winter, and save the trimmings for Christmas greenery. Mulch well and water during dry spells. Wear gloves; the spines are sharp.

quickId: Long, arching, sword-shaped fronds
One row of small leaflets on each side of the stem, finely scalloped at the edges
Thin, wiry, hair-like runners dangling from the plant
lookalikes: Tuberous sword fern (Nephrolepis cordifolia): stiffer, more upright fronds with small round tubers on the roots; invasive in the Southeast when planted in the ground.
facts: The classic Southern porch fern in hanging baskets.
The wiry runners root wherever they touch soil and start new plants.
A naturally occurring form of the native sword fern, first found in Boston in the 1890s.
care: Keep the soil evenly moist and give it bright shade, never hot afternoon sun. Bring it inside or into a garage when nights drop below about 40°F; a frost will kill the fronds. Brown, crispy fronds usually mean it's too dry. Trim them off at the base.

quickId: Massive, low, sweeping horizontal limbs, often wider than the tree is tall
Small, leathery, oblong leaves with smooth edges, dark green on top and grayish underneath, often slightly rolled under
Evergreen; limbs usually draped in Spanish moss and covered with resurrection fern
lookalikes: Laurel oak and water oak: taller and more upright, with thinner, shinier leaves and branches that angle upward rather than spreading out. Laurel oak drops most of its leaves in early spring.
facts: Called "live" oak because it stays green all year, dropping old leaves only in spring as new ones push out.
The ferny growth on the upper sides of the limbs is resurrection fern; it curls up brown in dry weather and turns green again after rain.
Live oaks can live for centuries. Its dense wood framed the hull of the USS Constitution ("Old Ironsides").
South Carolina's state tree is the palmetto, but live oak is the Lowcountry's signature tree.
care: Have an ISA-certified arborist handle any limb work on a tree this size. Avoid piling soil or mulch against the trunk, driving or parking over the root zone, or trenching near it; most damage to old live oaks comes from root disturbance. Spanish moss and resurrection fern don't hurt the tree.

quickId: Gray, curly, thread-thin strands hanging in long tangled curtains
Grows on tree limbs (especially live oak and cypress) with no roots in soil
Strands are made of tiny scaly leaves; turns greener when wet
lookalikes: Usnea (beard lichen): pale green-gray, stiffer, and shorter, with a stretchy white core inside each strand. Spanish moss strands have no white core.
facts: Not a moss: it's a bromeliad, a relative of the pineapple.
Takes water and nutrients from rain, fog, and dust; it doesn't feed on the tree.
Tiny pale-green flowers in late spring are easy to miss.
Historically gathered, cured, and used to stuff mattresses, furniture, and early car seats.
care: Harmless to healthy trees. Heavy clumps on a weak limb can add weight, but there's no need to remove it. Chiggers can live in moss that has fallen to the ground, so handle it with care.

where: Upper side of front-yard live oak limb (outlined in photo)
quickId: Small fern, a few inches tall, growing in mats along the tops of big tree limbs
Fronds have a single row of short, rounded lobes on each side
Curls up brown and shriveled in dry weather; flat and green after rain
lookalikes: Moss or lichen on limbs, when it's curled up dry. After a rain the fern fronds are unmistakable.
facts: Can lose most of its water, look completely dead, and revive within hours of a rain.
Grows on the bark without feeding on the tree, and is especially common on old live oaks.
It flew on Space Shuttle Discovery in 1997 so scientists could study its revival in zero gravity.
care: Leave it alone. It doesn't harm the tree. After a rain is the best time to see it.

quickId: Tall grass (3–6 ft) growing on beach dunes
Drooping golden seed heads of flat, oat-like spikelets that dangle from the tips of tall stalks
Long, narrow leaves that roll inward in dry weather
lookalikes: Bitter panicum (Panicum amarum): bluish-green, wider leaves and airy, narrow seed heads with tiny seeds, no flat dangling spikelets. American beachgrass: stiff, dense spike-like heads; more common farther north.
facts: Its deep, spreading roots trap blowing sand and build and hold the dunes that protect the coast.
Protected by South Carolina law: it's illegal to pick, cut, or damage sea oats.
Seed heads ripen golden in late summer and fall and feed birds and other wildlife.
care: Enjoy from the walkovers. Stay off the dunes and never pick the seed heads.

quickId: Small, flat-topped clusters of tiny tubular flowers (yellow, orange, pink, red, often changing color as they age)
Rough, sandpapery, toothed leaves in opposite pairs; pungent smell when crushed
Clusters of round green berries that ripen glossy black
lookalikes: Verbena: similar flower clusters but lower-growing, with narrower or more deeply cut leaves. Native buttonsage (Lantana involucrata) has small white-lavender flowers and is more common farther south.
facts: A butterfly magnet that blooms from late spring until frost.
Leaves and unripe green berries are poisonous to people, pets, and livestock.
Thrives in heat, drought, sun, and salt spray, so it's a beach-town staple.
care: Frost will knock it back to the ground. Leave the dead stems over winter for protection, then cut it to about 6–12 in. in early spring once new growth appears at the base. Full sun, little water once established, and no need to fertilize. Many named varieties are sterile and don't set berries.

quickId: Floats free on the water in dense mats, not rooted in the bottom
Thick, glossy, rounded leaves in rosettes
Swollen, spongy, bulb-like leaf stalks that act as floats; showy lavender flower spikes in summer
lookalikes: American frogbit (Limnobium spongia): native, smaller heart-shaped leaves with a spongy pad underneath but no swollen stalks. Pickerelweed: native, rooted in the mud along banks, with tall arrow-shaped leaves and blue flower spikes.
facts: Native to South America and considered one of the world's worst aquatic weeds.
Mats can double in size in a couple of weeks, blocking boats and choking out native plants and fish.
Listed as a prohibited invasive aquatic plant in South Carolina, so it's illegal to sell, possess, or move it.
Frost knocks it back, but it often survives Lowcountry winters in sheltered spots.
care: Don't take any home for a pond, and clean plant bits off boats, kayaks, and trailers before moving to another waterway. Report large infestations to the SC Department of Natural Resources.

quickId: Large, thick, leathery leaves (5–10 in.), glossy dark green on top
Undersides fuzzy and rusty brown, so from below the tree looks bronze
Smooth gray bark; huge white fragrant flowers in late spring and summer, then cone-like pods with bright red seeds in fall
lookalikes: Sweetbay magnolia (Magnolia virginiana): native, smaller leaves with silvery-white undersides instead of rusty brown. Cherry laurel and loquat have smaller or toothed leaves.
facts: Evergreen and native to the Southeast coastal plain; state flower of Mississippi and Louisiana.
Drops old leaves through the year, especially in spring. Its crunchy leaves are slow to break down.
Birds, squirrels, and wild turkeys eat the red seeds.
The cut branches are a classic Southern Christmas decoration.
care: Lower branches can sweep the ground; leaving them helps shade the shallow roots and hides the dropped leaves. Grass rarely grows under it. Prune only dead or crossing limbs, in late winter or right after bloom. It needs little else once established.

quickId: Diamond- or heart-shaped leaves with a long, narrow pointed tip, on long slender leaf stalks
Leaves flutter like a poplar's and turn brilliant red, orange, and purple in fall
Clusters of waxy white seeds in fall and winter that look like popcorn
lookalikes: Eastern redbud: heart-shaped leaves too, but rounder with no drawn-out tip. Cottonwood/poplar: similar fluttering leaves but toothed edges; tallow leaf edges are smooth.
facts: Brought from China in the 1700s for the waxy seed coating, used for candles and soap.
One of the most invasive trees in the Southeast: birds spread the seeds, and it takes over marsh edges, ditches, and woods.
Its milky sap, leaves, and seeds are toxic and can irritate skin.
Listed among the worst invasive plants in South Carolina by the SC Exotic Pest Plant Council.
care: Best removed. Pull seedlings when small. For larger trees, cut low and immediately treat the stump with an herbicide labeled for it (or hire a tree service); otherwise it resprouts from the stump and roots. Wear gloves because of the sap.

quickId: Evergreen foliage of tiny, scale-like leaves pressed along the twigs, with some short prickly needles on young growth
Reddish-brown bark that peels in long, thin, stringy strips
Small, frosty blue berry-like cones on female trees; strong cedar scent when foliage is crushed
lookalikes: Bald cypress: soft, flat, feathery needles in two rows that turn rusty and drop in fall; red cedar stays green all winter. Arborvitae: flat, fan-like sprays of foliage.
facts: Not a true cedar: it's a juniper.
The fragrant, rot-resistant heartwood is used for cedar chests, closet linings, fence posts, and pencils.
Birds such as cedar waxwings and bluebirds eat the blue "berries" in winter.
Very tough: handles salt spray, wind, drought, and poor sandy soil.
care: Needs almost nothing. Avoid planting it near apple or crabapple trees, since it hosts cedar-apple rust, a fungus that shows up as orange jelly-like galls in spring. Remove dead lower branches anytime.

quickId: Feather-shaped (pinnate) fronds that arch strongly and curve back toward the thick trunk
Blue-gray to silvery-green leaflets in a V along each frond
Short, stout trunk covered in old leaf-base stubs; spiny leaf stalks
lookalikes: Sabal (cabbage) palmetto, SC's state tree: fan-shaped leaves, not feathery, on a tall, straight trunk. Canary Island date palm: much bigger, greener, and stiffer fronds on a huge trunk.
facts: Native to southern Brazil and Uruguay; one of the most cold-hardy feather palms, surviving into the teens °F.
In summer it bears clusters of orange fruit that taste like a mix of pineapple, apricot, and banana and make good jelly, hence "jelly palm."
Fallen fruit can get messy and attract insects.
care: Remove only fully brown fronds, leaving a few inches of stalk; never cut green fronds. Wear gloves, as the stalks have spines. Yellowing older fronds often mean low potassium or magnesium; a palm fertilizer in spring and summer helps.

quickId: Glossy star-shaped leaves with 5 (sometimes 7) pointed lobes and finely toothed edges
Leaves alternate along the twig (maples' are paired); fragrant when crushed
Spiky round seed balls ("gumballs") that hang on the tree and litter the ground
lookalikes: Red maple: lobed leaves too, but in opposite pairs, with 3 main lobes and coarser teeth, and winged "helicopter" seeds instead of gumballs.
facts: Native across the Southeast and among the most colorful fall trees here: yellow, orange, red, and deep purple, often all on one tree.
Its resin ("sweet gum") was once chewed like gum and used in folk medicine.
Older twigs sometimes grow corky wings.
Goldfinches and other birds eat the tiny seeds from the gumballs.
care: Tough and low-maintenance. The main nuisance is the spiky gumballs, which roll underfoot and dull mower blades; rake them up in winter and spring. Keep it away from sidewalks and patios, as its surface roots can lift pavement.

quickId: Tall, straight trunk with a rounded crown high up; lower trunk often bare
Needles 6–9 in. long in bundles of 3, slightly twisted, in bushy tufts at branch tips
Thick bark in reddish-brown scaly plates; prickly brown cones 3–6 in. long
lookalikes: Longleaf pine: much longer needles (10–18 in.) in big drooping tufts and larger cones (6–10 in.). Slash pine: needles in 2s and 3s, glossy cones. Count needles per bundle and measure cone length.
facts: The most common pine in the Southeast and a mainstay of the timber and paper industry.
In fall, pines shed their older inner needles, which turn orange-brown before dropping; the tips stay green. That's normal, not disease.
Fallen needles become pine straw, the classic Southern mulch.
"Loblolly" is an old Southern word for a muddy low spot, where these pines often grow.
care: Little care needed. Have an arborist check large pines near the house for lightning damage, cracks, or lean. Signs of trouble are browning of whole branches or the whole crown, or pitch tubes (popcorn-like resin blobs) on the bark, which can mean pine beetles.

quickId: Small oval leaves (1–2 in.) in opposite pairs, gray-green with irregular creamy-white edges
Thin, arching, twiggy branches forming a loose, airy shrub
Fuzzy young twigs; small, strong-scented white flowers in spring and blue-black berries
lookalikes: Waxleaf ligustrum (Ligustrum japonicum): much larger, thicker, glossy leaves, usually solid green. Variegated elaeagnus: silvery speckled leaf undersides and alternate leaves. Variegated boxwood: smaller, stiffer leaves and dense growth.
facts: Plain green Chinese privet is one of the worst invasive shrubs in the Southeast, forming thickets in woods and along streams.
The variegated form spreads less aggressively, but it often reverts to plain green shoots, and its seedlings can come up all green.
Birds spread the berries widely.
care: Cut out any all-green shoots as soon as they appear. Shear or thin anytime in the growing season; it takes hard pruning well. Pull seedlings, and consider replacing it with a native shrub.
